10081,The provider opens (incises) and drains the contents of a pilonidal cyst  a nest of hair and debris that forms at the base of the spine; the procedure requires extra time and technique to perform. Explanation After appropriate preparation and anesthesia  with the patient lying in the prone (face down) position  the provider incises the area over a pilonidal cyst just above the central buttock crease. She opens the cyst and drains or scrapes out the contents. If the cyst is extremely enlarged  as it would likely be to require a complicated incision and drainage (I&D)  it may require a layered closure and drain. She irrigates the wound thoroughly and sutures the incision  in layers if necessary. She may pack the wound with gauze and allow it to heal by secondary intention or leave a tube inserted into the wound before closing  which will be attached to a pump to help drain any fluid that continues to form. A pilonidal cyst is a cyst or abscess near or at the bottom of the coccyx (tip of the spine) just above the buttock crease that contains hair and skin debris; pilonidal means nest of hair; also referred to as a pilonidal abscess or pilonidal sinus. Terminology Excision; resection: Removal of tissue  organ  or other structure in whole or in part. Incision and drainage (I&D): Surgical procedure in which cysts  abscesses  or other lesions containing infective material are incised (cut into) and the infective material drained; the procedure typically includes irrigation (washing out) of the affected part. Pilonidal cyst: A cyst or abscess near or at the bottom of the coccyx (buttocks) that contains hair and skin debris; pilonidal means nest of hair; also referred to as a pilonidal abscess or pilonidal sinus. Secondary intention healing: Healing process in which a wound is left to heal on its own. Tips Unlike 10080  code 10081 generally requires drain placement  more extensive packing  or subsequent wound closure. See 11770 to 11772 for excision of a pilonidal cyst or sinus. 10120,The provider removes a foreign body such as a thorn  piece of wood  sliver of glass or fishook  from the lower layer of skin. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider uses appropriate instrumentation to remove the foreign body. As this is a simple incision  it is not complicated; therefore  this type of foreign body removal requires no dissection. The provider incises the skin around the foreign body to better expose it and then removes it with forceps. The provider closes the incision and cleans and dresses the wound. Terminology Foreign body: Object originating from outside the body or displaced from another location from within the body  such as shards of metal  splinters of wound  slivers of glass  or a bone fragment. Subcutaneous tissue: Tissue found just below the skin  or dermis  layers; there are three layers of skin known as epidermis  dermis  and hypodermis; subcutaneous tissue is the lowermost layer called hypodermis. Tips For a complicated I&D of a foreign body  report 10121. Be sure the documentation supports a complicated procedure. A complicated I&D may require more extended exploration  imaging guidance  and/or layered closure of the wound. Read Less,https://www.aapc.com/codes/cpt-codes/10120,2025-11-05T09:19:00.209584Z

10140,The provider makes an incision into the hematoma  seroma  or other collection of fluid and bluntly penetrates it to allow fluid evacuation. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider makes an incision into a hematoma  seroma  or other collection of fluids and bluntly penetrates it to allow the fluid to evacuate  with or without the necessity of packing. The provider closes the incision primarily  meaning at that session  or he leaves the incision to heal without closure. The provider may place pressure dressing over the skin. Terminology Hematoma: Swelling or mass of blood confined to an organ  tissue  or space; caused by a break in a blood vessel. Incision and drainage (I&D): Surgical procedure in which cysts  abscesses  or other lesions containing infective material are incised (cut into) and the infective material drained; the procedure typically includes irrigation (washing out) of the affected part. Seroma: A pocket of serous fluid  the watery component of blood  that sometimes develops in the body after surgery. Read Less,https://www.aapc.com/codes/cpt-codes/10140,2025-11-05T09:19:42.027083Z

Explanation The provider cleans and isolates the area on the skin and inserts a needle into the fluid deposit area. He then withdraws the fluid or pus through the needle aspiration device. The provider applies antibiotics and dressing. The provider may place a pressure dressing over the area. Terminology Abscess: Localized collection of pus of any size in any location  and as such represents an infection. Aspiration: Withdrawal of fluids or tissue from the body. 11000,The provider uses surgical instruments to debride the dead tissue in skin for up to 10 percent of the body surface. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider cleans the area of infected skin. The provider then performs debridement by cutting away the dead tissue using surgical instruments like a scalpel or scissors. The provider performs debridement until he sees healthy bleeding on the skin edges. The provider then controls bleeding  applies an antibiotic  and dresses the wound. Use this code for debridement of up to 10 percent of the body surface. Terminology Debridement: Removal of dead  damaged  or infected tissue to facilitate natural healing of the remaining healthy tissue in an organ. Eczema: Common medical condition characterized by rough patchy skin with itching and inflammation. Tips Use +11001 as an add??n code for each additional 10 percent of the body surface. This code is for surgical debridement. For removal of devitalized tissue (nonselective debridement) from wound(s)  without anesthesia (e.g.  wet??o??oist dressings  enzymatic  abrasion  larval therapy)  ... per session  see 97602. Larval therapy refers to maggot therapy. This code also does not include dermabrasion; for dermabrasion services  see codes 15780 to 15787. 11047,The provider uses surgical instruments to remove dead  infected tissue from bone as well as the epidermis  dermis  and subcutaneous tissue  muscle  and/or fascia if needed. She performs this service at the same session  as a separately reportable debridement procedure of an initial 20 cm2. This code represents up to 20 cm2 of additional area. Explanation At the same session that the provider performs a primary procedure for bone debridement of 20 cm2  the provider performs debridement for up to an additional 20 cm2. When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider uses a scalpel  scissors  or other tools to remove large areas of necrotic affected tissue from bone as well as the epidermis  dermis  subcutaneous tissue  muscle and/or fascia as needed. Once she reaches healthy tissue  she closes the wound by primary closure or in layers or may leave the wound to heal by secondary intention. Terminology cm2: Abbreviation for square centimeter  a metric unit of measure of area; the 2 is usually superscripted; 1 cm equals approximately 0.39 inches  or just over a third of an inch  so a square centimeter would be 1 cm x 1 cm; alternative sq cm. Debridement: Removal of dead  damaged  or infected tissue to facilitate natural healing of the remaining healthy tissue. Dermis: Layer of skin between the epidermis and subcutaneous tissues. Epidermis: Thin outer layer of the skin. Fascia: A fibrous tissue sheet surrounding the body under the skin and enclosing muscles. Necrotic tissues: Dead cells or tissues in a body area that occur due to various external factors such as an injury  infection  or toxoid. Secondary intention healing: Healing process in which the wound is more open and prone to infection because it?? left to heal on its own. Subcutaneous tissue: Tissue found just below the skin  or dermis  layers; there are three layers of skin known as epidermis  dermis  and hypodermis; subcutaneous tissue is the lowermost layer called hypodermis. Tips Because +11047 is an add??n code  payers will not reimburse you if you report it without an appropriate primary code for debridement: 11044. 11055,The provider removes a single benign hyperkeratotic lesion by using surgical instruments like a scalpel or curette. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider evaluates the size  depth  and location of the benign hyperkeratotic lesion. She uses a scalpel  curette  blade  or a spoon??haped surgical instrument to trim or pare down the lesion. The provider applies antiseptic to the site and  if necessary  removes the pressure points by fitting padding on the site. Terminology Benign: Condition or growth that is not cancerous in nature. Callus: Caused by skin pressure; mainly appears on soles of feet or hands as an area of toughened skin. Corn: Caused by skin friction; mainly appears on top or side of toes as a small thickened area with a dense central area. Curette: Surgical instrument used for scraping skin or tissues. Hyperkeratosis: Dead skin that builds up from repeated or prolonged pressure to the skin; examples are corns and calluses. Tips Use 11056 when the service involves 2 to 4 lesions. Use 11057 when the service involves more than 4 lesions. Note that 11055  11056  and 11057 should not be used to report the destruction of skin tags or cutaneous vascular proliferative lesions (see 17110 and 17111). Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider evaluates the location and size of the skin tags. She uses forceps  scissors  or a blade to remove the skin tags. She may remove smaller tags painlessly without applying anesthesia. She applies an antibiotic after removing skin tags. Use this code for removal of skin tag lesions  up to 15. Terminology Skin tag: Also known as acrochordon; small  cutaneous  benign projections; commonly seen on the neck  face  armpit  and groin. 11300,The provider removes one epidermal or dermal lesion of 0.5 cm diameter or less from the trunk  arms  or legs. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  the provider evaluates the lesion on the trunk  arms  or legs. She then uses a scalpel blade to remove the lesion from its base by performing a horizontal slicing motion. She performs shaving typically to the middle dermis layer  without disturbing the subcutaneous tissue. The provider controls bleeding by cauterization  without any suturing. Use this code for a skin lesion of 0.5 cm diameter or less. Terminology Cauterization: Use of heat or chemicals to destroy abnormal cells or seal a wound. Dermis: Layer of skin between the epidermis and subcutaneous tissues. Epidermis: Thin outer layer of the skin. Subcutaneous tissue: Tissue found just below the skin or dermis layer; there are three layers of skin known as epidermis  dermis  and hypodermis; subcutaneous tissue is the lowermost layer called hypodermis. Tips For the same procedure on a lesion with a diameter 0.6 to 1.0 cm  see 11301. For the same procedure on a lesion with a diameter of 1.1 to 2.0 cm  see 11302. For the same procedure on a lesion with a lesion diameter over 2.0 cm  see 11303. If a provider removes multiple lesions of the same or different diameters during the same session  apply modifier 59  Distinct procedural service  to the code(s) for the additional lesion(s). To differentiate between codes for shaving and excision  look at the removal's depth. Technically  any time a provider removes skin tissue  it is an excision. For coding purposes  however  excision is narrowly defined as involving full thickness  or through the dermis  removal of a lesion. Shaving  in contrast  involves sharp removal without a full thickness dermal excision. Read the documentation carefully  and pay more attention to the removal's depth than to the terminology your physician uses. When reporting shaving procedures  you must not consider the size of any margin the physician removes with the lesion. In fact  the physician may not document  or even take  a margin of tissue during a shave. This is a crucial difference from coding for excisions. 11301,The provider shaves off a single epidermal or dermal lesion of 0.6 to 1.0 cm in diameter from the skin of the trunk  arms  or legs. Explanation When the patient is appropriately prepped and the area anesthetized  the provider holds a blade horizontal to the skin of the trunk  arms  or legs and moves it across a single lesion of 0.6 to 1.0 cm in diameter with a sawing motion. Shaving usually extends to the middle dermis without disturbing the subcutaneous tissue  followed by cautery to control bleeding  without any suturing. 11720,The provider surgically debrides (debulks or removes) 1 to 5 abnormal  diseased  or infected nails. Terminology Wound Dehiscence: The premature opening or breakage of a surgical suture in the wound. It is a surgical complication that results in poor wound healing and may involve infection. Tips If repair of wound dehiscence occurs during the postoperative (or global surgical) period of a previous procedure, be sure to append modifier 78 to the appropriate repair code. As such, wound dehiscence usually describes the opening of a previously sutured area (for example, an incision following surgery, wound repair, etc.). If a wound becomes infected, it will more likely dehisce due to the natural inflammatory process. Wound dehiscence code 12020 (Treatment of superficial wound dehiscence; simple closure) describes repair when there is no sign of infection. In this case, the surgeon simply debrides and irrigates the wound and closes it in a single layer. 17315,"Mohs surgery is a multistaged method of excising a malignant lesion layer by layer, along with histopathological assessment, to ensure negative malignancy of the margins. Excision is continued until the pathology results show negative results for malignancy. 19020,The provider performs a mastotomy (incision into the breast) and explores and/or drains a deep abscess in the breast. Explanation A deep abscess in the breast is generally identified and located through ultrasound. With the patient appropriately prepped and under general anesthesia  the provider makes a small incision in the skin above the abscess. She introduces a catheter to explore and drain the abscess. She may collect specimens of the drainage fluid for further diagnostic studies. She repeatedly irrigates and flushes the abscess cavity with sterile saline solution until the abscess is completely free from purulent material. She closes the wound with sutures. She may leave the catheter in place for a couple of days to facilitate saline instillation and drainage until no drainage occurs. Following which she may close the remaining opening with sutures or adhesive strips. An abscess in the breast is caused by the collection of pus due to an untreated bacterial infection and is most common during lactation. Mastitis or inflammation of the breast due to the accumulation of milk in the mammary ducts is another cause of abscess formation. Antibiotics in the initial stage can prevent infection and abscess formation. Once formed  the abscess may need surgical intervention such as incision and drainage for removal of the pus. Terminology Abscess: A collection of pus in a walled??ff sac or pocket  the result of infection. Antibiotic: Substance that inhibits or treats bacterial infections. Aspiration: Removal of fluid  gas  or other material through a tube attached to a suction device  often for laboratory analysis or combined with irrigation  the instillation of fluid to clean a wound or to wash out a cavity such as the abdomen  stomach  lungs  or joints; also  breathing in or sucking in food  fluid  or a foreign object into the airway. Mammary ducts: Ducts (tubes) that carry milk from the mammary glands to the nipples during lactation or secretion of milk; also known as Lactiferous duct  galactophorous ducts (milk ducts). 31367,The provider performs a subtotal (partial or extended near??otal) laryngectomy  removing the part of the larynx (voice box) above the vocal cords without radical neck dissection (excision of additional tissue and lymph nodes). Explanation After the patient is appropriately prepped and anesthetized  and prior to starting the main surgery  the provider performs a separate incision for tracheostomy that allows the patient to breathe during the surgery and the postoperative healing period. He dissects the thyroid cartilages to reach the diseased tissue. False vocal cords: Folds of mucous membrane enclosing the laryngeal vestibular ligament and separating the larngeal ventricle from the laryngeal vestibule (the part of the larynx above the vocal cords); false vocal cords are not directly involved in speech production; also called vestibular folds. Hyoid bone: A small bone at the base of the lower jaw that is shaped like the letter U and serves to support the tongue to facilitate speech and swallowing; it is the only bone in the human body that does not connect to any other bone and is instead connected only through muscle tissue. Supraglottis: The area of the pharynx (throat) between the glottis (the vocal cords) and the epiglottis (the flap of tissue at the back of the throat that prevents food from entering the larynx and trachea. Suprahyoid muscles: Muscles above the hyoid bone  which is the bone that supports the tongue; muscles include digastrics  stylohyoid  geniohyoid  and the mylohyoid muscles. Thyroid cartilage: A firm structure that is present around the wind pipe and contains the voice box and forms the Adam's apple. 55700,"The provider biopsies the prostate gland with a special biopsy needle or during surgery for pathological examination. Report this code regardless of the approach  for example  transrectal  perineal  or transurethral. Explanation A prostate biopsy is a procedure in which small samples are removed from the prostate gland with a special biopsy needle or during surgery  to be tested for the presence of cancer or other abnormal cell growth. A prostate biopsy can be performed by several different methods: Transrectal approach: The skin over the surgical site is cleaned with an antiseptic liquid. The provider inserts a needle through the wall of the rectum and into the prostate to obtain tissue samples. These tissue samples are then sent to pathology for further examination. Transurethral approach: The provider inserts a cystoscope through the opening at the end of the penis and into the urethra. He then inserts instruments through the cystoscope and obtains tissue samples. These tissue samples are then sent to pathology for further examination. Perineal approach: The perineum is cleansed with an antiseptic. The provider inserts an ultrasound probe into the rectum to guide needle placement. He inserts a special biopsy needle through the perineum and into the prostate where he activates the needle and withdraws tissue  which he sends to pathology for further examination. Needle biopsy: The withdrawal of a tissue sample through the use of a specially designed needle without the need for an incision. Perineum: The surface area between the scrotum and anus in men  bounded by the thighs  and the external genitalia and skin between the genitalia and anus in women. Prostate: A small gland that is part of the reproductive system in males and located just below the urinary bladder; it secretes prostatic fluid  a component of semen.
